analysis.one_liner: Lets dairy farmers tax their own milk sales to fund a board that buys up surplus dairy products and exports them.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan dairy farmer proposal to shift milk-surplus costs off taxpayers died in committee after a year of hearings and subcommittee work, never reaching a House floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace some federal milk price support spending with a self-help program paid for by dairy farmers themselves. Farmers would pay up to 20 cents per hundredweight in deductions on every gallon of milk sold, and an 18-member Dairy Stabilization Board — mostly farmers and dairy industry leaders elected by producers — would use the money to pull surplus butter, cheese, and powder off the market, export them, and export dairy cattle, so the government's Commodity Credit Corporation would buy less. The bill set the program to run from 1994 through 1998 and extended related dairy deficit-reduction levies through 1998.
analysis.who_benefits: Dairy farmers are the direct beneficiaries: the board they elect would remove surpluses that drag down farm milk prices, producers who did not expand production would get refunds of the deductions, and federal budget levies on farmers would be redirected into tools the industry controls. Taxpayers would also gain somewhat, because the government's surplus-buying bill would shrink.

how_it_helps.text: The bill funds a producer-run Dairy Stabilization Board that removes surplus dairy products from the domestic market and disposes of them mainly through export sales, keeping surpluses from depressing farm milk prices [S2][S3].

Producers who did not increase their milk marketings would receive refunds of the deductions, and when the board wound up, any leftover money would be rebated to farmers who paid the market stabilization deduction [S3].

The bill's stated purpose is to cut net federal spending under the milk price support program by reducing Commodity Credit Corporation purchases of surplus dairy products, contributing to deficit reduction for fiscal years 1994 through 1998 [S2][S3].
It caps the butter purchase price at $0.65 per pound and sets a floor of $1.034 per pound for nonfat dry milk, reshaping how the government's support price is split between the two products [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Milk producers pay up to 20 cents per hundredweight in deductions on all milk sold, collected from their revenues under federal and state milk marketing orders, with civil penalties for anyone who fails to collect or remit. Consumers indirectly bear part of the cost, because pulling dairy products off the market supports higher milk prices, and large or expanding farms pay extra under targeted reductions on milk above their production base.

drawbacks.text: The Dairy Stabilization Board is an industry body: 12 of its 18 members are producers nominated through elections in which dairy cooperatives may cast bloc votes on behalf of their members, and the rest are dairy industry insiders. It would wield public-style market intervention powers with the Federal Advisory Committee Act expressly not applying to it, subject only to the Agriculture Secretary's approval [S3].

Removing dairy products from the domestic market and exporting them is a supply-management tool that supports milk prices; the bill's own consumer-protection clause promises fair prices to both producers and consumers, but consumers would face the upward price pressure the program is designed to create [S3].

Targeted reductions fall on milk marketed above a farm's established base, so new producers get a base of only 75 percent of their marketings and growing farms pay more than their established neighbors — a rule that favors incumbents [S3].

The program ran through 1998 with annual plans, a dedicated fund, and quarterly rate adjustments, adding a layer of administrative machinery (capped at $2 million or 5 percent of the annual budget) whose costs are ultimately borne by the farmers paying the deductions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For dairy farmers the trade was arguably a good one: money they were already paying in federal deficit levies would be redirected into a board they elect, with refunds for producers who don't expand. But the arrangement hands market-management power to an industry-dominated board, leans on export disposal of surplus products, and puts upward pressure on retail milk prices. Consumers get no direct benefit and bear the price-stabilization effect; taxpayers get only the indirect savings from fewer government purchases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, spent nearly a year in its Livestock Subcommittee through hearings and three mark-up sessions, and was forwarded to the full committee amended by voice vote on June 8, 1994 — but the full committee never acted, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Introduced July 15, 1993 by Rep. Volkmer with Rep. Gunderson, the bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its Livestock Subcommittee [S1][S5].
The subcommittee held hearings in July and October 1993 and requested and received executive comment from the USDA [S5].
The subcommittee held mark-up sessions in November 1993, April 1994, and June 1994, and on June 8, 1994 forwarded the bill to the full Agriculture Committee in amended form by voice vote [S5].
No further action was taken: the full committee never voted on the bill, the House never debated it, and it never received a vote in either chamber before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and the existing dairy program status quo: milk drinkers avoided a farmer-governed supply-management program that would have put upward pressure on retail prices, and the federal dairy support system continued unchanged rather than being restructured around an industry board.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and the dairy-program status quo

sides.party_line_note: No floor or committee votes were ever recorded; the bill's only measured support was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor joined by a Republican lead cosponsor and five cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans.

industries.note: Farmers would pay up to 20 cents per hundredweight in deductions on all milk sold, but the board they elect would remove surpluses and export products to support their milk prices, with refunds for producers who don't expand. Cooperative leaders would gain formal power: 12 of 18 board seats go to producer nominees chosen in elections where cooperatives can vote bloc-style for their members.

The board would pay export bonuses to move removed dairy products and dairy cattle abroad, and the bill requires actual export sales to be done by dairy cooperatives and international marketers rather than the board itself — creating paid contracts and bonus opportunities for the export trade.

Handlers would face civil penalties for failing to collect and remit the deductions, but a new federal milk order cost-sharing provision would reimburse handlers for the costs of sourcing supplemental milk or disposing of excess milk.

industries.industry: Federal dairy price support program (Commodity Credit Corporation and taxpayers)
industries.note: The program is designed to cut net federal spending by having producer-funded removals happen before the government has to buy surplus butter, cheese, and powder, reducing the government's surplus-purchase outlays through 1998.
